meta.title: Astra Vigil 2.0 | Team MANTA
meta.description: Astra Vigil 2.0 is an offline crew health console for deep-space missions. It compares each astronaut with their own baseline, flags drift early and cites NASA research. Team MANTA, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

earth.s: Home, and where the crew's data goes

hero.title: Astra Vigil 2.0
hero.tagline: A quiet watch over crew health when Earth is too far to answer.
hero.sub: Astra Vigil compares each astronaut with their own normal, flags drift while it is still small, and points to the NASA research behind the signal. It runs offline, never diagnoses, and keeps raw data with its owner.

challenge.title: The challenge
challenge.body: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 asks for health monitoring software for astronauts. A crew on a long mission cannot wait for a flight surgeon on Earth, so the software has to notice change on board, explain it carefully and respect the people it watches.

asks.v: A console that replays crew vitals as they arrive.
Deterministic rules against each person's own baseline, in a compute module with no language model.
Each alert cites related NASA OSDR and NTRS records and never diagnoses.
A 600-row simulated fixture with planted anomalies.
Apache-2.0 repository and a README that says the telemetry is simulated.

problems.title: Five problems, answered honestly
problems.intro: We split the challenge into five problems. For each one, this page says what the prototype does, where in the code it lives and what it does not do.

items.name: Communication delay
items.short: Earth cannot answer in time, so the ship has to watch for itself.
items.how: All detection runs on board. Only a coarse status (learning, normal, watch or alert) enters a store-and-forward outbox, and the outbox releases it after the light-time delay.
items.limit: The delay is modelled, not measured on a real link. Presets use Mars one-way light times from NASA delay-tolerant networking slides, 3.04 to 22.29 minutes.

items.name: Real-time detection
items.short: Catch drift on the day it happens, not in the post-flight report.
items.how: Each day's reading is compared with that person's own 30-day baseline. Rule S and Rule M fire with the exact numbers behind them. There is no machine learning in this path.
items.limit: Tested on simulated data only. Real physiology is messier than our noise model, and a slow drift can hide inside the baseline. Try the Ramp shape in the playground.

items.name: Team-level early warning
items.short: Notice when several crew members move together.
items.how: The commander view shows coarse status for the whole crew in one place, and every person's status is computed the same way.
items.limit: We make no accuracy claim for crew-wide warning. A shared cause, such as cabin air, is not modelled yet.

items.name: Privacy versus monitoring
items.short: Safety needs data. Dignity needs limits.
items.how: Three tiers are enforced on the server. Raw data stays with its owner, the medical designee sees trend direction only with consent, and the commander and ground see coarse status. Every access goes into a hash-chained audit log.
items.limit: The audit chain exposes edits but cannot stop someone with full file access from deleting it all. A real system needs hardware-backed keys.

items.name: Crisis prevention
items.how: Alerts arrive while a change is still small, about one day after onset in our tests, together with the NASA records linked to that signal. We never forecast an event.
items.limit: An alert is a prompt to look, not a finding. We do not claim to predict emergencies.

explore.intro: Pick a planet and fly to it. Spin the view, speed up time, and read the numbers that matter for a crew: distance, gravity, day length and radio delay. On a phone you can look around with the gyroscope or drop it into a Cardboard-style viewer. With a headset, enter VR.

system.name: Whole system
system.blurb: Every orbit is drawn on one plane and every planet moves at its true relative pace. Pick a body to fly to it.
system.crew: A crew's world grows with every step out: the Moon is seconds away by radio, Mars minutes, Saturn more than an hour.

sun.name: Sun
sun.blurb: Holds more than 99% of the Solar System's mass.
sun.crew: Flares and energetic particles from the Sun are a main radiation concern on deep-space trips. NASA's DONKI service logs them.

mercury.name: Mercury
mercury.blurb: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, with a very long day: one turn takes about 59 Earth days.
mercury.crew: Sunlight is about seven times stronger than at Earth, so heat control would be the main challenge.

venus.name: Venus
venus.blurb: A thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat. It is the hottest planet and spins backwards, very slowly.
venus.crew: Surface temperatures near 464 °C and crushing air pressure rule out landing. A crew would stay in orbit.

earth.name: Earth
earth.blurb: The only place known to host life. Its magnetic field and atmosphere shield everything on the ground.
earth.crew: Crews in low Earth orbit are still partly shielded by Earth's magnetic field. Beyond it, that help is gone.

moon.name: Moon
moon.blurb: Always shows the same face to Earth. Radio signals take about 1.3 seconds each way.
moon.crew: The proving ground for Artemis: close enough for near-real-time help, far enough to practise living away from home.

mars.name: Mars
mars.blurb: A cold, dry world with a thin atmosphere, about half Earth's width.
mars.crew: One-way radio takes 3 to 22 minutes, gravity is about 0.38 g and the thin air gives little radiation shielding. That is why crew health tools must work without Earth.

jupiter.name: Jupiter
jupiter.blurb: The largest planet. Its Great Red Spot is a storm that has been seen for well over a century.
jupiter.crew: Its radiation belts are intense, so even robot probes need heavy shielding.

saturn.name: Saturn
saturn.blurb: Famous for its wide ring system, made mostly of water-ice particles.
saturn.crew: One-way radio takes more than an hour even at the closest approach, so a crew there would make every decision alone.

uranus.name: Uranus
uranus.blurb: Tipped on its side, so each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight and then 42 years of darkness.
uranus.crew: Radio takes more than two hours one way.

neptune.name: Neptune
neptune.blurb: The farthest planet, with the fastest winds measured in the Solar System.
neptune.crew: Radio takes about four hours one way at best.

detector.title: How the detector decides
detector.intro: The science boundary of the project is one small Python file. It contains no language model and no hidden state. These are its steps, in order.

steps.title: Collect one summary per day
steps.body: Each row is one mission-day summary of six signals: resting heart rate, HRV, SpO2, sleep, core temperature and exercise. The demo replays 1 to 60 rows per second.

steps.title: Build a personal baseline
steps.body: The baseline is the last 30 usable days for that person and signal. At least 14 are needed. Until then the status is learning.

steps.title: Score today against it
steps.body: z = (today minus baseline mean) divided by baseline SD, with a minimum SD per signal so a very steady baseline cannot create absurd scores. Only the worse direction counts: heart rate and temperature up, HRV, SpO2, sleep and exercise down.

steps.title: Apply two rules
steps.body: Rule S: one signal at least 2.0 SD worse on 2 days in a row. Rule M: at least 2 different signals at least 2.5 SD worse within 48 hours, raised once when the pattern appears.

steps.title: Keep the baseline honest
steps.body: Days inside a confirmed episode are left out of the baseline, so a long problem cannot become the new normal. One-off blips stay in, because removing them made false alarms worse in our tests.

steps.title: Explain, never diagnose
steps.body: An alert shows its rule and numbers. The text comes from a template. An optional local language model may reword it, and its text is discarded if it uses diagnostic words or numbers that are not in the alert.

steps.title: Attach NASA context
steps.body: Cached OSDR and NTRS records related to the signal appear as reading material, not as proof.

validation.caveat: These numbers describe this detector on Gaussian noise with a mild day-to-day link. They say nothing yet about real astronauts. A false alarm every 40 days per person is also a cost: alerts are meant to be looked at, not trusted blindly.

architecture.title: System architecture
architecture.intro: Three layers: sense, think, act. Data flows left to right and every box is a real module in the repository. Select a box to read what it does.

nodes.name: Wearables
nodes.detail: In the hardware prototype a Polar H10 chest strap supplies heart rate and HRV and a wrist wearable supplies sleep and SpO2 trends. These are design choices, not tested together yet.

nodes.name: Cabin nodes
nodes.short: ESP32 with CO2 and climate sensors
nodes.detail: ESP32 boards with an SCD40 (CO2) and a BME280 (temperature, humidity, pressure) publish over MQTT on an offline router. They give context for a crew-wide cause. The detector does not use them yet.

nodes.name: Fixture replay
nodes.detail: The software demo reads simulated mission-day rows for six crew members, with known planted events, so detection can be scored against ground truth. Names and photos are the team's. Every vital is simulated and every row is marked simulated.

nodes.name: CSV import
nodes.detail: A command-line tool turns a CSV into a fixture and rejects values outside plausible ranges, for example SpO2 below 70 or heart rate above 220.

nodes.name: Mission engine
nodes.detail: Steps each crew member's data one day at a time, records baseline and score for every signal, and can rebuild any day deterministically.

nodes.name: Detector
nodes.detail: Personal baseline, z-score, two rules and baseline exclusion. Pure Python and NumPy. No network, no model.

nodes.name: Evidence mapper
nodes.detail: Maps a signal and direction to cached OSDR, NTRS and paper records and labels each as direct or adjacent. Works with no network.

nodes.name: Explainer and guard
nodes.detail: A template always produces the explanation. A local model, if you run one, may reword it, but the guard rejects diagnostic language and numbers that are not in the alert.

nodes.name: Privacy projector
nodes.detail: Builds a different view of the same moment for each role and checks consent. Raw values never leave the crew member's tier.

nodes.name: Outbox
nodes.detail: Holds coarse status until the light-time delay has passed. A schema check refuses any payload with fields outside the allow-list.

nodes.name: Audit log
nodes.detail: Each entry includes the hash of the one before it, so editing or deleting an entry breaks verification. Also holds consent records.

nodes.name: Crew console
nodes.detail: The crew member sees their own values, baselines, alerts and explanations with NASA references.

nodes.name: Medical designee
nodes.detail: Sees only trend direction per signal, such as drifting toward worse, and only for crew who consented.

nodes.name: Commander
nodes.detail: Sees coarse status for everyone in real time: learning, normal, watch or alert.

nodes.name: Ground
nodes.detail: Receives the same coarse status through the outbox after the light-time delay.

architecture.transport: FastAPI serves REST and WebSocket on the local machine. The console is plain JavaScript on canvas, with no framework and no CDN.
architecture.pick_hint: Select a box to see the details.

hub.title: NASA health data APIs
hub.intro: Crew health starts with NASA's own data: biology from spaceflight, research papers, space radiation, and the air and heat conditions on Earth. These are the NASA services we use or could use, each with a live fetch. Our server makes the request, and every answer says whether it is live, cached or unavailable.
hub.banner: Requests go from this site's server to NASA, only when you press Fetch. Your browser never contacts NASA.
hub.banner_off: Offline mode is on (VIGIL_OFFLINE). Nothing is sent to NASA. Answers come from cached records only.

osdr_search.name: OSDR study search
osdr_search.what: Search NASA's Open Science Data Repository for spaceflight biology studies: blood, muscle, bone, microbiome, immune data.
osdr_search.why: These studies are the evidence for what changes in a body in space, and so for which signals a monitor should watch.

osdr_meta.name: OSDR dataset details
osdr_meta.what: Look up one OSDR study by accession (for example OSD-569) in the Biological Data API: organism, mission, assays, release date.
osdr_meta.why: It shows exactly what a dataset measured before anyone builds on it.

ntrs.name: NASA Technical Reports (NTRS)
ntrs.what: Search NASA's technical reports and papers, including Human Research Program work.
ntrs.why: It finds the published findings on sleep, vision, radiation and isolation in crews.

donki.name: DONKI space weather
donki.what: NASA's Space Weather Database: solar flares, energetic particle events, geomagnetic storms, coronal mass ejections and notifications.
donki.why: Solar particle events are one of the main radiation risks on deep-space trips, so crews need warning.

eonet.name: EONET Earth events
eonet.what: Natural events NASA is tracking now: wildfires, volcanoes, dust and haze, storms, floods, temperature extremes.
eonet.why: Smoke, ash and heat waves affect health on the ground, and show how NASA data serves public health.

cmr.name: Earthdata CMR: data collections
cmr.what: Search NASA Earth science data collections, such as TEMPO air-quality data.
cmr.why: Air quality is a health measure on Earth. The same idea applies to cabin air.

power.name: POWER temperature and humidity
power.what: Daily air temperature and humidity at any point on Earth, from NASA's POWER project.
power.why: Heat and humidity drive heat stress, an everyday field health risk, and are a reference for habitat comfort.

images.name: NASA Image and Video Library
images.what: Search NASA's public images and videos.
images.why: It finds public material about astronaut health, exercise and medicine.

horizons.name: JPL Horizons: Earth-Mars light time
horizons.what: NASA/JPL's solar-system data service. We ask it where a planet is as seen from Earth, and read off the distance and the one-way light time for the next days.
horizons.why: It gives the real light delay for today instead of a fixed preset, so the 22 and 44 minute figures can be checked against NASA's own numbers.

dsn.name: Deep Space Network Now
dsn.what: NASA's live list of which Deep Space Network dishes are talking to which spacecraft, with signal direction and data rate.
dsn.why: It shows the real ground link that a delayed, coarse status message would travel through.

msg.unreachable: NASA could not be reached from this server (no internet, or the host is blocked).
msg.rate_limited: NASA says too many requests. The shared DEMO_KEY allows only a few calls per hour. Wait, or set NASA_API_KEY.
msg.offline_mode: Offline mode: no request was sent.
msg.unexpected_response: NASA answered, but not in the expected format.

hub.not_yet: Nothing fetched yet. Press the button.
hub.error: The site could not run this request:
hub.key_demo: Uses NASA's shared DEMO_KEY, which allows only a few requests per hour. Set the NASA_API_KEY environment variable for more.
hub.key_custom: Uses the NASA API key set on this server.
hub.check_note: Runs each API once with its default values.
hub.honest: Only the OSDR and NTRS answers are also bundled with the site, so only those can fall back to cached records. The other APIs show nothing when NASA cannot be reached. Nothing here is medical advice, and radiation or weather data are context, not a diagnosis.

platforms.title: The four NASA platforms
platforms.intro: NASA's data and APIs are public, and Space Apps needs no special key. NASA lists four platforms. Each service on this page is grouped under the closest one. Some services live on their own NASA sites.

api_portal.name: NASA API Portal
api_portal.what: Explore NASA's APIs and their documentation. An optional free key raises the request limit.

why.hrp: NASA's Human Research Program studies how spaceflight affects the body and mind. It is the research setting for any crew-health monitor, including this one.

nasa.title: NASA data and the dataset list
nasa.intro: Astra Vigil uses three NASA services as references, and the list below shows every dataset and source the project touches. Search it, filter it, open a row for details, or download it.

services.name: NASA OSDR
services.use: Open Science Data Repository. We cache 9 SpaceX Inspiration4 datasets (OSD-569 to OSD-575, OSD-630, OSD-656) as adjacent context for signals.

services.name: NASA NTRS
services.use: Technical Reports Server. We cache reports on heart rhythm in long flights, sleep, cardiorespiratory change and behavioural health, plus peer-reviewed papers.

services.name: NASA DONKI
services.use: Space weather: flares, geomagnetic storms and coronal mass ejections. Planned as cabin-radiation context.
services.status: Sync code is ready. The cache is empty in this build and needs a free key from api.nasa.gov.

nasa.records_title: Every dataset and source in the project
nasa.how: When an alert fires, the evidence mapper lists the records linked to that signal and direction. They are reading material beside the numbers. They are not proof that a rule is clinically meaningful.
nasa.gap: Core temperature has no thermoregulation-specific record in the cache, only adjacent inflammation datasets. We say so instead of stretching a match.
nasa.search_ph: Search by ID, title or mission
nasa.none: Nothing matches. Clear the search or pick another type.

hardware.note: We have not tested this hardware together, and we have not independently verified the two precedents beyond their sources.

tech.title: Technical system description
tech.intro: The stack is deliberately small so a team can read all of it in an afternoon.

stack.v: One SQLite file: audit chain, consent, outbox
Vanilla JavaScript modules, canvas, and a bundled copy of Three.js for the 3D views (galaxy, Solar System, WebXR and phone VR). No framework, no CDN, no remote fonts
WebSocket ticker at 10 Hz; replay speed 1 to 60 rows per second
Template always; optional local model through Ollama behind a guard
Verified in a headless browser: only requests to localhost
33 automated tests in the console project, plus tests for this website

pipeline: A row of six values arrives for each crew member.
The detector scores each value against that person's baseline.
Rules S and M decide whether to raise an alert.
The explainer writes the text and the evidence mapper adds NASA records.
The projector builds one view per role and checks consent.
Coarse status goes to the outbox; every access goes to the audit log.
The WebSocket pushes the result to the console.

limits.title: What this is, and what it is not
limits.intro: A project about health should be careful with its claims. This is our list.
is: A working software prototype with a deterministic detector
Offline-first, with all NASA references bundled
Built and tested on simulated data from four fictional crew
isnt: A medical device, or a source of diagnosis or treatment advice
Validated on real astronaut or patient data
Flight-qualified, or tested on the hardware plan
A predictor of emergencies. It detects change; it does not forecast
todo: The live NASA sync has only been tested with mocked responses, because the build environment could not reach NASA directly.
The DONKI space-weather cache is empty in this build.
Detection numbers come from a simple noise model. Real data will be harder.
The next step is a review by a clinician and a trial with consenting volunteers wearing real sensors.

journey.title: The journey, with the five problems
journey.intro: A simulated crew leaves the space station, passes Earth and flies to Mars. Move the slider or press Play. At five points on the way, one of the five problems this project answers shows up.
journey.route_note: Schematic route, not a flight plan. The transit is drawn as 259 days, the computed time of a minimum-energy (Hohmann) Earth-Mars transfer; real missions take roughly 6 to 9 months depending on the launch window and the trajectory. Distance from Earth follows the farthest-case light time from NASA's delay-tolerant networking slides (NTRS 20160011483), so it is an upper bound for that moment, not today's distance.

stages.text: On the station, ground doctors are a radio call away. The monitor starts here: it learns each person's own 30-day baseline, so that later it can catch a drift on the day it happens rather than in the post-flight report.

stages.light: one-way light time about a minute
stages.text: Six people share one small cabin, the same air and the same stress. When several of them drift the same way at once, that points to a shared cause, not six separate problems. The detector watches for exactly that.

stages.light: one-way light time a few minutes
stages.text: Wearables record everything about a body for months. The ship enforces three tiers: raw numbers stay with their owner, the medical designee sees trend direction only with consent, and the commander and Earth see only a coarse status.

stages.light: one-way light time heading toward 22 minutes
stages.text: A question to Earth now needs about 44 minutes for its answer. The ship cannot wait, so it decides on board and sends only a thin status through a store-and-forward outbox.

stages.light: one-way light time 3 to 22 minutes, depending on where Mars is
stages.text: There is no quick rescue and no quick answer. What helps is an early alert while a change is still small, with the NASA records behind it. We detect early; we never claim to predict an emergency.

delay.title: Mars to Earth and back: 44 minutes
delay.intro: A status packet leaves Mars at the speed of light. At the farthest distance it needs about 22 minutes to reach Earth. Earth's answer needs another 22 minutes to come back. The crew has waited about 44 minutes in total.
delay.phase_idle: Press Play to send the packet.
delay.phase_done: The answer is back. {rt} minutes have passed on the real clock.
delay.demo_note: The 3D clock runs {x} times faster than real time so you can watch it. The numbers shown are real minutes.
delay.decide: During these {rt} minutes the crew has to decide alone. This is why Astra Vigil watches on board.

live.title: Today's real value
live.unavailable: NASA JPL Horizons could not be reached from this server, so the fixed range from NASA's delay-tolerant networking slides is used.
live.source: Source: NASA/JPL Horizons (quantity 21, one-way light time), fetched by the server. Your browser never contacts NASA.
live.range: NASA's range: {near} to {far} minutes one way
live.computed_note: NASA JPL Horizons could not be reached, so this value is computed on the server from approximate orbital elements (JPL, Standish). It is an estimate, typically within a few tenths of a minute, and not NASA live data.
live.source_computed: Source: computed on the server from approximate orbital elements (JPL, Standish). It is an estimate, not a NASA value; it switches to JPL Horizons (quantity 21) whenever that answers. Your browser never contacts NASA.

crew.title: The crew: six people, all simulated
crew.intro: Team MANTA plays the crew. Names and photos are the team's; every number is invented. Move the day slider to watch coarse status change over 600 mission days. Pick one person to see what only that person would see: their own numbers (tier 0).
crew.view_status: Commander and Earth view: coarse status only (tier 2)
crew.none_planted: No planted change for this person
crew.worse: SD in the worse direction from own baseline
crew.note: Alerts include chance alerts: the detector has a known false-alarm rate. Nobody else's raw numbers are ever returned by the server, only coarse status.

compare.title: With and without the software
compare.intro: The same simulated change in {name}'s {signal}, shown twice. Without software, nobody watches the trend, so it is noticed at the next scheduled health review. With Astra Vigil, the real detector raises the alert on board. The two 3D lanes are drawn to the real numbers.

events.noticed_at_review: Noticed at the next health review

assump: The review interval defaults to 14 days, NASA's ISS Private Psychological Conference interval (NTRS 20170003866). That a change is only noticed at the next review, and that a Mars crew would keep the same interval, are assumptions of this scenario. Change it with the slider.
With the software, the alert is raised on board, so the crew does not wait for Earth. Earth still receives a coarse status after the light-time delay.
Light times are the Mars one-way values from NASA's delay-tolerant networking slides (NTRS 20160011483).
compare.tiny: Earth's answer comes {rt} minutes after the status leaves the ship. On this time axis that is a hairline. The days lost before anyone looks matter far more.
compare.schematic: Curves are schematic: how long the change goes unaddressed
compare.caveat: The detector is the real one and the data is simulated. One planted event is a demonstration, not a clinical trial.
compare.tabs_scale: Scale: each lane is drawn to the same time axis.

ship.title: Inside the ship: where the software lives
ship.intro: A cut-away of the crew ship. Select a module to see what it does, which hardware it uses, which file holds the software, and what is built, planned or only a concept. The moving dots are the real data flow.

modules.name: Crew quarters: wearables
modules.what: Each crew member would wear a chest strap (heart rate, HRV) and a wrist device (sleep, SpO2 trend) and stream raw numbers to the ship computer.
modules.hardware: Polar H10 chest strap. A wrist wearable (device not fixed).
modules.software: Today the numbers come from the simulated fixture replay and the CSV import tool, which rejects implausible values. A live Bluetooth reader is planned, not built.
modules.note: Raw values stay in this on-board loop and never go to Earth.

modules.name: Cabin sensor nodes
modules.what: Small boards report CO2, temperature, humidity and pressure over MQTT on an offline network. They give context for a crew-wide cause such as stale air.
modules.hardware: ESP32 boards with an SCD40 (CO2) and a BME280 (temperature, humidity, pressure), plus an offline router running Mosquitto.
modules.software: The detector does not use cabin data yet. It is context only.
modules.note: Honest limit: this is a plan. We have not tested the hardware together.

modules.name: Vigil Core: the ship computer
modules.what: Reads every reading, keeps each person's own 30-day baseline, runs Rule S and Rule M, links the signal to NASA records, writes the explanation and applies the three privacy tiers. It works with no network.
modules.hardware: Bench: Raspberry Pi 5 or Jetson Orin Nano. Flight concept: redundant A/B units with ECC memory, so one unit can fail without losing the watch.
modules.software: Mission engine, detector, evidence mapper, explainer with a guard, privacy tiers and the outbox.
modules.file: engine.py, compute/detect.py, evidence.py, explain.py, privacy.py, store.py
modules.note: The software is built and tested. The flight hardware is a concept.

modules.name: Crew console and medical bay
modules.what: Shows each person their own numbers and alerts (tier 0), the medical designee the trend direction with consent (tier 1), and the commander the live coarse status of everyone (tier 2).
modules.hardware: Any tablet or laptop on the cabin network.
modules.software: The web console, with the tier rules enforced on the server.
modules.note: Every access goes into a hash-chained audit log.

modules.name: Comms bay: outbox to the dish
modules.what: Only the day, the time and each crew member's id and coarse status may enter the store-and-forward outbox. It holds each message for the light-time delay and then sends it. Anything with raw vitals is rejected.
modules.hardware: Flight concept: delay-tolerant networking over the ship's high-gain antenna.
modules.software: The outbox simulation and its payload check.
modules.note: The outbox is built and tested. The radio and the real delay-tolerant network are a concept.

modules.name: Earth: mission control
modules.what: Receives the same coarse status after one-way light time. Ground never receives raw vitals. Through this site's server hub it can also pull NASA data: OSDR, NTRS, DONKI and JPL Horizons.
modules.hardware: NASA's Deep Space Network dishes. They are not part of our prototype.
modules.software: The NASA data hub and the Earth-Mars link endpoint.
modules.note: Our server calls NASA. Your browser never does.

ship.how_title: What the software does, step by step

how.name: Read
how.text: A reading arrives from a wearable or from the fixture replay. Implausible values are rejected.

how.name: Learn
how.text: The detector compares it with that person's own 30-day baseline. The first 14 days only learn.

how.name: Check
how.text: Rule S and Rule M look for a shift, with the exact numbers behind it. No machine learning, no diagnosis.

how.name: Explain
how.text: A template writes the explanation and links the signal to NASA records, marked direct or adjacent.

how.name: Filter
how.text: The three privacy tiers decide who sees what. Raw numbers stay with their owner.

how.name: Queue
how.text: Only a coarse status enters the outbox, which holds it for the light-time delay.

how.name: Send
how.text: Earth gets the status after one-way light time. Nothing in the ship waits for that.

ship.added_title: What the software adds to the ship
ship.added: Without it, the ship only logs numbers and a doctor reads them later, after Earth has answered. With it, the ship watches every person every day, explains each alert, and tells Earth only what Earth is allowed to know.

legend.flow: Moving dots show the data flow

updates.title: What changed in this update
updates.intro: This page now shows where the software sits inside the ship, how it is different from before, and which NASA services it connects to. Here is the full list, from the first console to this release.

versions.name: Astra Vigil 2.0 console
items: Four fictional crew and the Rule S and Rule M detector on each person's own 30-day baseline.
Three privacy tiers and a hash-chained audit log.
Store-and-forward outbox for the Earth link.

versions.name: Six crew and planning
items: Six crew members, a hazard ring, an automatic plan and a report.

versions.name: More indicators, more security
items: Ten health indicators in the console.

versions.name: Real NASA data in the console
items: A real NASA data part, a daily chart and six crew photos.

versions.name: Mission 3D theatre
items: The 3D section is now five views: the journey from the space station to Mars with the five problems, the 44-minute round trip, the crew, with and without the software, and the inside of the ship.
The website crew is now the six Team MANTA members, with photos.
Ten NASA services instead of eight: JPL Horizons and Deep Space Network Now were added, and DONKI got a fallback address.

honest: All crew data is simulated. Nothing here has been tested on real astronauts.
The NASA connections are tested against mock answers. The server could not reach NASA while this release was built, so run a live check from the NASA APIs section.
